title: Stuffed courgettes
subtitle: Koosa with spiced rice and lamb filling
excerpt: Stuffed courgettes are small round or elongated courgettes cored and filled with spiced lamb and rice, then simmered in a light tomato broth until the courgette is tender and the filling cooked through. The work is mostly in the coring, which a small teaspoon handles easily.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Koosa mahshi documented as a home dish across the Levant and Egypt, made throughout the summer when courgettes are plentiful. Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). Detailed notes on the coring technique and proportions.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Prepare and stuff the courgettes a day ahead, then refrigerate. Bring to room temperature and add the broth before cooking.

content.text: Stuffed courgettes are a Lebanese and Syrian summer staple: the courgettes are cored to a thin shell, filled with a mixture of raw lamb mince, rice, and warm spices, then simmered in a shallow tomato broth until everything cooks together. The broth steams the filling and keeps the courgettes from drying out. It is patient, careful cooking that rewards properly: the courgette flesh becomes very tender and the filling is dense and savoury inside.

items.prepNote: small, ideally round or short elongated ones
optional, for richness in the filling

content.text: Trim the stem end from each {{courgette}} and cut a small lid from the top (round ones) or just trim the top (elongated ones). Use a small apple corer or a teaspoon to scoop out the flesh, leaving a wall about 5 mm thick all the way round. Keep the scooped flesh for another use or discard.
Work carefully to avoid piercing the skin. Hold the courgette upright and rotate it against the corer rather than pushing straight through.

Mix {{lamb-mince}}, {{long-grain-rice}}, grated {{onion}}, {{allspice}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{black-pepper}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}} together in a bowl. If using {{unsalted-butter}}, add it here and mix well.
Fill each courgette cavity loosely to about two-thirds full. The rice will expand during cooking, so do not pack tightly or the courgette will split.
Combine {{tinned-tomatoes}}, {{tomato-puree}}, crushed {{garlic}}, {{sea-salt-fine}}, and 400 ml of water in a wide, deep saucepan. Stir to combine.

Lay the stuffed courgettes in the broth in a single layer, open end up if round, or on their sides if elongated. The broth should come halfway up the courgettes; add more water if needed. Bring to the boil.

Cover tightly, reduce the heat to a low simmer, and cook for 45 to 50 minutes until the courgettes are very tender when pierced and the filling is cooked through. Check occasionally to make sure the broth has not dried up, adding a splash of water if needed.
Leave to rest for five minutes before serving. Serve in shallow bowls with some broth spooned over and {{plain-yoghurt}} alongside.

items.cause: Filling packed too tightly; the rice expanded and cracked the skin
items.fix: Fill to two-thirds only. If a courgette splits, it is still edible: transfer it to a bowl and serve with broth.

items.symptom: The filling is still raw after fifty minutes
items.cause: Broth dried out or heat too low
items.fix: Check the broth level every fifteen minutes. Keep it at a steady simmer, not just a whisper. Add boiling water from the kettle if it dries up.

items.symptom: The broth is thin and watery
items.cause: Too much water added or the tomatoes were watery
items.fix: Remove the lid for the last ten minutes to reduce the broth. Or simply ladle it off; the courgettes will still be delicious.

items.symptom: The courgettes are very soft but the rice is still chalky
items.cause: Not enough liquid reached the filling
items.fix: Pierce the courgettes gently with a skewer to allow more steam and liquid into the cavity, and cook for another ten minutes covered.

content.text: Stuffed vegetables are central to Levantine and Egyptian cooking. Courgettes, peppers, aubergines, vine leaves, and cabbage are all stuffed with rice and meat fillings. Koosa mahshi (stuffed courgette) is a summer dish in Lebanon and Syria, made when pale green koosa courgettes reach the markets. The pale green koosa has a thin skin and holds its shape during cooking. Small elongated courgettes are the best UK substitute. This is a weekend lunch dish, not a quick weeknight meal.
